body:
A birthday party can be a lot for an autistic child. Noise, crowds, bright decorations and a full programme can turn a happy day into a hard one. A few small changes make a big difference.

Share a simple plan beforehand. Tell guests what will happen and when, and show your child the plan too. Pictures work well for younger children.

Set up a quiet corner. A blanket, cushions and a few favourite toys in a calmer room give anyone a place to rest when it gets too much.

Keep the noise down. Skip the balloons that pop, keep music at a gentle level and avoid surprise noise makers.

Offer familiar food. Have at least one dish you know your child enjoys, without pressure to try new things.

Keep it short. Two hours is plenty. Ending on a good note matters more than fitting everything in.

title: Demo: Five ways to make a birthday party autism friendly

body:
Many autistic adults want to work and have a lot to offer. Often what stands in the way is not the job itself but the way the workplace is set up.

Clear instructions help everyone. Put tasks in writing, say exactly what done looks like and give deadlines as dates, not as soon as possible.

Interviews can be adjusted. Sharing questions ahead of time or offering a practical task instead of a panel interview lets candidates show their real skills.

Small changes to the space matter. A desk away from the kitchen, permission to wear headphones or a quiet room for breaks can make a full day manageable.

Ask, do not assume. Every autistic person is different. The best ally asks what would help and then follows through.
